questions.text: How much of your work follows repeatable steps with predictable inputs and outputs?
questions.why_asked: Tasks that repeat the same way each time are the easiest for software to take over.

questions.text: How much time do you spend transferring, checking, reconciling, or filing records in a standard format?
questions.why_asked: Filling in forms and keeping records is some of the first work AI tools take on.

questions.text: How often must you physically handle equipment, materials, land, animals, food, or people to complete the work?
questions.why_asked: Physical work that changes from day to day is hard for software alone to do.

questions.text: How often do you work on-site where weather, terrain, machinery, traffic, or changing conditions affect your next move?
questions.why_asked: Work out in the field needs someone on the spot who can react to what they find.

questions.text: How often does success depend on another person trusting your judgment, care, discretion, or integrity?
questions.why_asked: When people need to trust the person in front of them, the job usually stays human even if AI helps.

questions.text: How often are you personally accountable for decisions that materially affect safety, rights, money, health, or livelihoods?
questions.why_asked: A company can let AI do the analysis and still need a person to answer for the decision.

questions.text: How often must you create an original direction, interpretation, design, performance, or solution rather than adapt a template?
questions.why_asked: AI can produce plenty of options, but choosing the right one for the moment is still your call.

questions.text: How much of your output is produced by finding, cleaning, summarizing, or transforming digital information?
questions.why_asked: Work done entirely on a screen is easy for AI to reach, but it can also save you a lot of time.

questions.text: How often do you combine incomplete or conflicting evidence to diagnose a problem or choose a course of action?
questions.why_asked: AI can help you think a problem through, but unclear cases still need someone to check the answer.

questions.text: How confidently can you use AI tools while checking their work for errors, bias, privacy, and safety?
questions.why_asked: Knowing how to use AI well is what turns it from a threat into an advantage.

questions.text: How often must you explain complex or sensitive information so a specific audience can act on it?
questions.why_asked: Writing for people you understand is harder to copy than turning out generic text.

questions.text: How often do you negotiate trade-offs among people with different goals, power, or constraints?
questions.why_asked: Negotiating means reading people, knowing what they want, and having the authority to agree.

questions.text: How often must you interpret rules, standards, permits, or professional obligations rather than simply follow a checklist?
questions.why_asked: Regulated work usually needs a qualified person to sign off and take responsibility.

questions.text: How often must you notice hazards and act safely when the situation differs from the standard procedure?
questions.why_asked: When something goes wrong and safety is at stake, someone has to be there to make the call.

questions.text: How often must you read emotion, reduce tension, motivate someone, or respond with genuine care?
questions.why_asked: Difficult conversations with upset or worried people are still strongly human work.

questions.text: How often does your result depend on local language, culture, informal networks, terrain, or market knowledge that is poorly documented?
questions.why_asked: Knowing your area, your people and how things really work locally is not something AI is trained on.

questions.text: How often do you decide what to sell, set prices, find customers, manage cash, or take business risk yourself?
questions.why_asked: If you set your own prices and choose your own customers, you control more of what happens next.

questions.text: How much of your value comes from understanding a client’s unstated needs and adapting the service in real time?
questions.why_asked: Working out what a client actually needs is harder to standardise than a simple transaction.

questions.text: When tools or customer expectations change, how confidently can you learn a new method and apply it to real work?
questions.why_asked: How quickly you pick up new tools is the one thing here you can change straight away.

questions.text: How much does your work rely on expertise built through substantial practice, certification, or hard-to-transfer experience?
questions.why_asked: The better you know your field, the quicker you spot when AI gets something wrong.

questions.text: How predictable is your work environment from one day or case to the next?
questions.why_asked: It is easier to automate work in a steady setting than work where conditions keep changing.

questions.text: Which best describes how your work creates income?
answers: Paid for volume or standard tasks
I own the business or assets
questions.why_asked: Being paid per task carries more risk than being paid for results or owning the work.

questions.text: How often do you set direction, allocate resources, coach others, or take responsibility for a team’s outcome?
questions.why_asked: Leading means motivating people, weighing trade-offs and answering for how it turns out.

questions.text: During the past three years, how much have digital tools changed the tasks people in your role perform?
questions.why_asked: What has already changed in your job tells us more than any prediction about the future.
